my_notes: Smelly when wet. Best paper for many precise techniques, due to the hard surface sizing.
content:
Ideal paper for botanical paintings, but it smells bad when water is applied onto it. 
Its quality is non-negotiable, it can take a lot of layers, it allows for a subtle glow in the colors when using it. 
It can take a LOT of layers. It's one of the papers with the absolute best performance for botanical painting when using the layering technique. 
The colors are absorbed immediately due to the cotton content, and it is great for all dry or wet techniques. 
It allows for the most precise lines achievable along with Saunders Waterford Hotpress paper. 
The smoothness of the paper's surface is almost unsurpassed by any other paper on the market, and it allows for light to pass through color, even after several layers. It can be used with or without masking fluide or tape, without any issues, and is ideal for use with a lightpad. It takes well to graphite too, or colored pencils. 
Avoid mixing colors directly on the paper's surface, as the high absorption will disturb the mixing process. 

**From the manufactor: Info about paper coating/sizing:**
Sized to the core with natural gelatin: a process exclusive to ARCHES®. ARCHES® is the only paper mill in the world to gelatin size its watercolour paper “to the core”. Even if it is soaked for a long time, the paper will still retain enough gelatin not to become too absorbent.
source: https://arches-papers.com/arches-range-of-papers/watercolor-and-wet-techniques/arches-aquarelle/

my_notes: Overrated product when it comes to price and general performance.
content:
The paper can not take as many layers as the Arches 300gsm hotpress paper. The sizing on the surface is different, which makes it difficult to work with for botanical painting. It feels like a board more than a paper, and it's not easy to cut out or transfer images onto with a lightpad either. After first experience, this paper will only be used if nothing else is available. The price/performance ratio is simply too bad, especially for the associated price tag. Sort of smelly when water is added to the surface.

Clean or crisp edges are very difficult to obtain for this paper, which is contradictory to its purpose - precise or detailed paintings. It needs considerable time to dry before new layers are applied or the pilling effects will begin to show on the surface. 
The surface itself is not as smooth as the 300gsm, but rather soft and scratchy. 

One thing it is good at though: Letting the colors glow - and it NEVER buckles.

my_notes:
Can be rough on brushes with natural hairs, especially when scrubbing occurs. 
Smelly when wet...
content:
Ideal for any type of paints that uses granulation! This paper is the classic go-to paper for any larger subject that does not require precise details (unless the subject is zoomed-in on). The color subdues the paint, while still allowing for light to transfer through the fibers and upward, aka light from within. Price/performance ratio is in the classic end, yes, it's expensive - but very satisfying for more "rough" effects or subjects. 

It's natural white color is not the brightest to work on, but retains the light effect, allowing the paints to breathe and flow. 

Ideal subjects can be anything from dreamy, blurry and loose florals/birds/plants/skies or a stormy sea - and to metal objects such as steam trains, lanterns or steampunk items. 
It's one of the best papers for wet-in-wet techniques, as it can hold a LOT of water. It allow the paint to flow, bloom and spread out, especially if it has granulation. Ideal for loose or impressionist techniques, but a bit difficult for crisp lines using either graphite, colored pencils or brushes.
The grainy surface can take a toll on soft haired brushes, so it's advisable to check this, perhaps using a synthetic blend or pure synthetic brush, depending on the brush type/brand.

my_notes: Not a staple, only tried once so far, but great price-performance ratio.
content:
One of the newer papers on the market - only available from Aart De Vos (online) in DK. The paper is very hard sized on the surface and smooth - but not as smooth as Arches HP 300gsm. Still, it holds up to a bit of layering before the layers below begin to dissolve. It does not smell when water is added to the surface.
It has a high degree of whiteness, just as Saunders Extra White, but it feels rather thin to the touch. It allows for light to pass through from below to a quite satisfying degree, better than Arches hotpress 300gsm. 
It's ideal for detailed or botanical subjects, and takes well to masking fluid. It's easy to transfer subjects to using a lightpad, and takes well to graphite or colored pencils. 

### From the manufactor:
Baohong Masters’ has a unique slow absorption rate, allowing artists more time to manipulate colour and pigment. This property aligns with traditional Chinese painting techniques that require precise control over colour flow. The paper’s controlled absorbency allows for the most subtle gradations essential in delicate watercolour painting techniques.

 - Sizing: A meticulous sizing process, both internal and external, using traditional gelatine, was crucial for controlling paint flow and for preventing buckling. 
- Performance: The paper readily accepts multiple washes without buckling or pilling, allowing for seamless blending and lifting techniques. 
- Longevity: The Acid-free and pH neutral paper is designed to withstand the test of time, preserving artwork for generations.

my_notes: Only used for drafts or low-effort paintings
content:
This paper is the beginner-friendly paper. It is cheap, and paints lifts easily. It's great for initial practise, and the cellulose content makes it easier to see brush strokes. 
The paper weight of 200gsm makes it easier to transfer outlines to using lightpads, but it also buckles easily. Water control is essential if using this paper. 
Light grain surface makes it suitable for almost all subjects and techniques, when the purpose is to just practise, have fun and not do serious work.

**From the manufactorer:**
Montval® paper was designed by the famous painter Gaspard Maillol, nephew of the sculptor Aristide Maillol, and manufactured by Canson® at his request in the early 20th century. Since then, this paper has acquired new qualities.  
One of them is its great erasability: corrections can be made easily, cleaning the paper with water, using a sponge or a brush. There is no trace of watercolour left and the paper can be worked again.  
Easy to use, it is accessible and suitable for everyone.

my_notes: Let layers dry between painting sessions to avoid lifting of color from the previous layers
content:
The first and only hotpress cellulose paper owned. Very smooth surface, easy to obtain clean, crisp and clear edges, but too many layers will make the paint below dissolve if not completely dry due to the cellulose content and low absorption quality of this paper. 
Colors pops and appear bright, it is very white and allows the light to pass through. 
It takes extremely well to graphite and colored pencils though, and is usable with both masking fluid and masking tape, as well as lightpad. 
The cellulose content shows brush lines more readily, and is not ideal for e.g. botanical watercolor subjects.
It is fun to play with, when the purpose is not too serious, or used for mixed media effects. Will probably work well with acrylics, but not watercolor!

**From the manufactor:**
https://www.speedballart.com/fluid-hot-press-blocks/
Made of 140lb (300gsm), high alpha-cellulose paper able to offer the qualities of 100% cotton at a more affordable price. Two-sided binding allows for easy removal of one sheet at a time and eliminates the need to stretch or secure edges with tape

my_notes: Do not paint on the backside (smooth side) - pills too fast and layers beneath dissolve
content:
Suitable for masking fluid and masking tape. This paper - although very thick, has many purposes, but the heavy weight makes it difficult to use with a lightpad. It is very sturdy, and has mainly been used to try out new techniques, or used for painted color cards. Its pristine white color makes the colors pop out of the paper, as does not absorb as much paint due to the cellulose content. It behave sort of like Hahnemühle Expression paper made from 100% cotton. 
Perfect for paintings with a loose and not too precise painting style. 
Ideal for granulating paints to work optimally. 
Also usable with e.g. guache, charcoal etc. 
**Important**: Using the smoother backside increases the risk of the paper pilling if more than 1 or 2 layers are applied.

**From the manufactorer:**
A high quality watercolour board with a matt surface structure in 425 gsm. This paper quality is acid-free, lightfast and extremely resistant to ageing and suitable for all wet painting techniques such as watercolour, gouache, tempera and acrylic.

my_notes: Impossible to obtain sharp details. Will only flow and bloom and is best for expressive, loose style painting
content:
Say goodbye to sharp edges with this paper! 
Impossible to control the painting process, if precision or sharp edges are the desired goal. It will be impossible to control the paints, but works great for impressionist style paintings, dreamy or blurry subjects/landscapes or other, spreads the paint very easily. Ideal for subjects such as the sea, stormy clouds, stormy skies with granulating paints, wet-in-wet techniques and dreamlike effects. Also ideal for natural subjects, or loose-style flower paintings. 

**Manufactor's description:**
Expression Watercolour – the natural-white 100-percent cotton, surfaced sized paper, is suitable for all wet-painting techniques and etching. Expression Watercolour features surface sizing. Colours stand out excellently on the paper and impress with their natural brilliance, thus giving every subject its very own, unique presence. Masking fluids or masking tape can be used and removed residue-free, while wet colours can be easily corrected or taken off.

Expression Watercolour is acid free, light-resistant and features extreme longevity. The surface is eraser resistant due to the surface sizing.

my_notes: Very soft. Only used a little so far (July 2026)
content:
Kristina Rapohina's own paper from her own brand, only available on her website (see references). 
The surface is very soft and a bit rougher than traditional hotpress papers, but there is almost no drying shifts, and it's easy to achieve the light-from-within effects, especially with flowers or other delicate/thin objects. The paper can be used for detailed subjects, such as botanical paintings, animal furs, leaves, trees - all sorts of detailed work basically. The paper needs to be completely dry before adding extra layers, as the layers below will begin to dissolve.
The paper is prone to pilling though, and scrubbing is not advisable. If corrections needs to be made, it's best to use the lifting method of dapping a dry towel onto the rewet surface the needed amount of times to remove stains.
The color retention is very good though, and this paper would also work with graphite, charcoal and guache.
It's versatile but very soft surface, works best with soft and natural brush hairs, such as (Kolinsky) sable, squireel (natural or synthetic) or the like.

my_notes: Can't take too many layers. Budget paper for practise of having fun. Not for serious work.
content:
Practise paper - not archival and not the best paper. Only available from Galleri Roholt (Private label paper)
Fine to use as a test drive or used for low-commitment subjects with less precision work. 
Too many layers will make the layers dissolve, best for practise or low-value efforts to have fun with. Takes well to graphite, easy to transfer subjects to with a lightpad or other. Also ideal for e.g. colored pencil practises.
Due to the 100% cotton content, colors seems to be absorbed or sucked into the layers, due to the soft sizing on the surface. Works impressively well with black ink!
It's not ideal for subjects that require a lot of layers, as the paint below will start to dissolve after too many layers or glazes.

my_notes: My all time favorite paper, soft sizing and surface, too stiff brushes may ruin paper surface
content:
A clear favorite, due to its budget friendly price-performance ratio and in general it's clean and solid performance. It's one of THE best papers for many detailed and precise botanical paintings, as it allows the paint to have that special, inner glow that makes the colors seem lit from within when using it. 
It's archival, UV resistant and the quality is indisguisable. It allows for a lot of scrubbing, corrections, layers and glazes, while still keeping the edges clean, firm and crisp. It lets the colors glow from within, and is very smooth to the touch. 
It absorbs colors a smidgeon slower than Arches hotpress 300gsm, and has great color absorption.
It's easy to transfer images to using a lightpad, and takes incredibly well to any type of graphite pencils, colored pencils and charcoal. 
Its surface compared to e.g. Arches hotpress 300gsm is a bit softer, as less sizing is used - so it's recommended to use a brush with softer or natural hairs, like kolinsky sable and squirrel hairs (natural and/or synthetic). 
It absorbs less color than e.g. Arches from the first washes. 
### From the manufactorer:
Saunders Waterford® is an exquisite watercolour paper, traditionally made on a cylinder mould machine. This is the superior quality watercolour paper made by St Cuthberts Mill and comes with the Royal Watercolour Society’s endorsement. Made using 100% cotton, the highest quality papermaking material, to high archival standards. Each sheet is buffered with calcium carbonate to help defend finished pieces of work from discolouration caused by acids present in atmospheric pollution.

Its attractive surface is created using natural woollen felts that give it a distinctive random texture. The surface is sized in gelatine making it strong and resilient to scrubbing, and other rough treatments.

Available in White and High White shades.
